title: Poor Folk
text: April 8th

title: Poor Folk
text: MY DEAREST BARBARA ALEXIEVNA,--How happy I was last night--how immeasurably, how impossibly happy!

title: Poor Folk
text: That was because for once in your life you had relented so far as to obey my wishes.

title: Poor Folk
text: At about eight o’clock I awoke from sleep (you know, my beloved one, that I always like to sleep for a short hour after my work is done)--I awoke, I say, and, lighting a candle, prepared my paper to write, and trimmed my pen. Then suddenly, for some reason or another, I raised my eyes--and felt my very heart leap within me!

title: Poor Folk
text: For you had understood what I wanted, you had understood what my heart was craving for.

title: Poor Folk
text: Yes, I perceived that a corner of the curtain in your window had been looped up and fastened to the cornice as I had suggested should be done; and it seemed to me that your dear face was glimmering at the window, and that you were looking at me from out of the darkness of your room, and that you were thinking of me.

title: Poor Folk
text: Yet how vexed I felt that I could not distinguish your sweet face clearly!

title: Poor Folk
text: For there was a time when you and I could see one another without any difficulty at all.

title: Poor Folk

title: Poor Folk
text: What sort of a tenement, do you think, is this?

title: Poor Folk
text: Formerly, as you know, I used to live in absolute stillness--so much so that if a fly took wing it could plainly be heard buzzing. Here, however, all is turmoil and shouting and clatter. The PLAN of the tenement you know already. Imagine a long corridor, quite dark, and by no means clean. To the right a dead wall, and to the left a row of doors stretching as far as the line of rooms extends. These rooms are tenanted by different people--by one, by two, or by three lodgers as the case may be, but in this arrangement there is no sort of system, and the place is a perfect Noah’s Ark.

title: Poor Folk
text: Most of the lodgers are respectable, educated, and even bookish people.

title: Poor Folk
text: In particular they include a tchinovnik (one of the literary staff in some government department), who is so well-read that he can expound Homer or any other author--in fact, ANYTHING, such a man of talent is he!

title: Poor Folk
text: Also, there are a couple of officers (for ever playing cards), a midshipman, and an English tutor.

title: Poor Folk
text: But, to amuse you, dearest, let me describe these people more categorically in my next letter, and tell you in detail about their lives.

title: Poor Folk
text: As for our landlady, she is a dirty little old woman who always walks about in a dressing-gown and slippers, and never ceases to shout at Theresa.

title: Poor Folk
text: I myself live in the kitchen--or, rather, in a small room which forms part of the kitchen.

title: Poor Folk
text: The latter is a very large, bright, clean, cheerful apartment with three windows in it, and a partition-wall which, running outwards from the front wall, makes a sort of little den, a sort of extra room, for myself.

title: Poor Folk
text: Everything in this den is comfortable and convenient, and I have, as I say, a window to myself.

title: Poor Folk

title: Poor Folk
text: Do not think, dearest, that in all this there is any hidden intention.

title: Poor Folk
text: The fact that I live in the kitchen merely means that I live behind the partition wall in that apartment--that I live quite alone, and spend my time in a quiet fashion compounded of trifles. For furniture I have provided myself with a bed, a table, a chest of drawers, and two small chairs. Also, I have suspended an ikon. True, better rooms MAY exist in the world than this--much better rooms; yet COMFORT is the chief thing.

title: Poor Folk
text: In fact, I have made all my arrangements for comfort’s sake alone; so do not for a moment imagine that I had any other end in view.

title: Poor Folk
text: And since your window happens to be just opposite to mine, and since the courtyard between us is narrow and I can see you as you pass,--why, the result is that this miserable wretch will be able to live at once more happily and with less outlay.

title: Poor Folk
text: The dearest room in this house costs, with board, thirty-five roubles--more than my purse could well afford; whereas MY room costs only twenty-four, though formerly I used to pay thirty, and so had to deny myself many things (I could drink tea but seldom, and never could indulge in tea and sugar as I do now).

title: Poor Folk
text: But, somehow, I do not like having to go without tea, for everyone else here is respectable, and the fact makes me ashamed.

title: Poor Folk
text: After all, one drinks tea largely to please one’s fellow men, Barbara, and to give oneself tone and an air of gentility (though, of myself, I care little about such things, for I am not a man of the finicking sort).

title: Poor Folk
text: Yet think you that, when all things needful--boots and the rest--have been paid for, much will remain?

title: Poor Folk
text: Yet I ought not to grumble at my salary,--I am quite satisfied with it; it is sufficient.

title: Poor Folk
text: It has sufficed me now for some years, and, in addition, I receive certain gratuities.

title: Poor Folk
text: Well good-bye, my darling.

title: Poor Folk
text: I have bought you two little pots of geraniums--quite cheap little pots, too--as a present.

title: Poor Folk
text: Perhaps you would also like some mignonette?

title: Poor Folk

title: Poor Folk
text: Also, do not misunderstand the fact that I have taken this room, my dearest.

title: Poor Folk

title: Poor Folk
text: The snugness of the place has caught my fancy.

title: Poor Folk
text: Also, I shall be able to save money here, and to hoard it against the future.

title: Poor Folk

title: Poor Folk
text: Nor must you despise me because I am such an insignificant old fellow that a fly could break me with its wing.

title: Poor Folk
text: True, I am not a swashbuckler; but perhaps there may also abide in me the spirit which should pertain to every man who is at once resigned and sure of himself.

title: Poor Folk

title: Poor Folk
text: I have now covered close upon a whole two sheets of notepaper, though I ought long ago to have been starting for the office.

title: Poor Folk
text: I kiss your hands, and remain ever your devoted slave, your faithful friend,

title: Poor Folk
text: P.S.--One thing I beg of you above all things--and that is, that you will answer this letter as FULLY as possible.

title: Poor Folk
text: With the letter I send you a packet of bonbons.

title: Poor Folk
text: Eat them for your health’s sake, nor, for the love of God, feel any uneasiness about me.

title: Poor Folk
text: Once more, dearest one, good-bye.

title: Poor Folk
text: April 8th

title: Poor Folk
text: MY BELOVED MAKAR ALEXIEVITCH,--Do you know, I must quarrel with you. Yes, good Makar Alexievitch, I really cannot accept your presents, for I know what they must have cost you--I know to what privations and self-denial they must have led.

title: Poor Folk
text: How many times have I not told you that I stand in need of NOTHING, of absolutely NOTHING, as well as that I shall never be in a position to recompense you for all the kindly acts with which you have loaded me?

title: Poor Folk
text: Why, for instance, have you sent me geraniums?

title: Poor Folk
text: A little sprig of balsam would not have mattered so much--but geraniums! Only have I to let fall an unguarded word--for example, about geraniums--and at once you buy me some!

title: Poor Folk
text: How much they must have cost you!

title: Poor Folk
text: Yet what a charm there is in them, with their flaming petals!

title: Poor Folk
text: Wherever did you get these beautiful plants?

title: Poor Folk
text: I have set them in my window as the most conspicuous place possible, while on the floor I have placed a bench for my other flowers to stand on (since you are good enough to enrich me with such presents).

title: Poor Folk
text: Unfortunately, Thedora, who, with her sweeping and polishing, makes a perfect sanctuary of my room, is not over-pleased at the arrangement.

title: Poor Folk
text: But why have you sent me also bonbons?

title: Poor Folk
text: Your letter tells me that something special is afoot with you, for I find in it so much about paradise and spring and sweet odours and the songs of birds.

title: Poor Folk
text: Surely, thought I to myself when I received it, this is as good as poetry!

title: Poor Folk
text: Indeed, verses are the only thing that your letter lacks, Makar Alexievitch.

title: Poor Folk
text: And what tender feelings I can read in it--what roseate-coloured fancies!

title: Poor Folk

text: Ah, Makar Alexievitch, you neither speak of nor give any account of what you have spent upon me.

title: Poor Folk

title: Poor Folk

title: Poor Folk
text: For instance, what has made you go and take the room which you have done, where you will be worried and disturbed, and where you have neither elbow-space nor comfort--you who love solitude, and never like to have any one near you?

title: Poor Folk

title: Poor Folk

text: Do you wish, then, to persuade me that your whole existence has been passed in loneliness and want and gloom, with never a cheering word to help you, nor a seat in a friend’s chimney-corner?

title: Poor Folk

title: Poor Folk
text: April 9th

title: Poor Folk
text: MY DEAREST MAKAR ALEXIEVITCH,--Are not you, my friend and benefactor, just a little ashamed to repine and give way to such despondency?

title: Poor Folk
text: And surely you are not offended with me?

title: Poor Folk
text: Ah!

title: Poor Folk
text: Though often thoughtless in my speech, I never should have imagined that you would take my words as a jest at your expense.

title: Poor Folk
text: Rest assured that NEVER should I make sport of your years or of your character.

title: Poor Folk
text: Only my own levity is at fault; still more, the fact that I am so weary of life.

title: Poor Folk
text: What will such a feeling not engender?

title: Poor Folk
text: To tell you the truth, I had supposed that YOU were jesting in your letter; wherefore, my heart was feeling heavy at the thought that you could feel so displeased with me.

title: Poor Folk
text: Kind comrade and helper, you will be doing me an injustice if for a single moment you ever suspect that I am lacking in feeling or in gratitude towards you.

title: Poor Folk
text: My heart, believe me, is able to appraise at its true worth all that you have done for me by protecting me from my enemies, and from hatred and persecution.

title: Poor Folk
text: Never shall I cease to pray to God for you; and, should my prayers ever reach Him and be received of Heaven, then assuredly fortune will smile upon you!

title: Poor Folk
text: Today I am not well.

title: Poor Folk
text: By turns I shiver and flush with heat, and Thedora is greatly disturbed about me....

title: Poor Folk
text: Do not scruple to come and see me, Makar Alexievitch.

title: Poor Folk
text: How can it concern other people what you do?

title: Poor Folk

title: Poor Folk
text: April 12th

title: Poor Folk
text: DEAREST MISTRESS BARBARA ALEXIEVNA,--I pray you, my beloved, to tell me what ails you.

title: Poor Folk
text: Every one of your letters fills me with alarm.

title: Poor Folk
text: On the other hand, in every letter I urge you to be more careful of yourself, and to wrap up yourself warmly, and to avoid going out in bad weather, and to be in all things prudent.

title: Poor Folk
text: Yet you go and disobey me!

title: Poor Folk
text: Ah, little angel, you are a perfect child!

title: Poor Folk
text: I know well that you are as weak as a blade of grass, and that, no matter what wind blows upon you, you are ready to fade.

title: Poor Folk
text: But you must be careful of yourself, dearest; you MUST look after yourself better; you MUST avoid all risks, lest you plunge your friends into desolation and despair.

title: Poor Folk
text: Dearest, you also express a wish to learn the details of my daily life and surroundings.

title: Poor Folk
text: That wish I hasten to satisfy.

title: Poor Folk
text: Let me begin at the beginning, since, by doing so, I shall explain things more systematically.

title: Poor Folk
text: In the first place, on entering this house, one passes into a very bare hall, and thence along a passage to a mean staircase.

title: Poor Folk
text: The reception room, however, is bright, clean, and spacious, and is lined with redwood and metal-work.

title: Poor Folk
text: But the scullery you would not care to see; it is greasy, dirty, and odoriferous, while the stairs are in rags, and the walls so covered with filth that the hand sticks fast wherever it touches them.

title: Poor Folk

text: The smell is abominable.

title: Poor Folk

title: Poor Folk
text: As to the disposition of the rooms, I have described it to you already.

In fact, I have no intention of going there again, since every one is for gambling, and for nothing but gambling. Even the literary tchinovnik gives such parties in his room--though, in his case, everything is done delicately and with a certain refinement, so that the thing has something of a retiring and innocent air.

title: Poor Folk
text: In passing, I may tell you that our landlady is NOT a nice woman.

title: Poor Folk

title: Poor Folk

title: Poor Folk

title: Poor Folk

title: Poor Folk
text: A red-haired, swine-jowled, snub-nosed, crooked lout, he is for ever wrangling with Theresa, until the pair nearly come to blows.

title: Poor Folk

title: Poor Folk

title: Poor Folk
text: Sometimes, too, certain things are done of which it would be shameful for me to speak.

title: Poor Folk
text: In particular, hardened though I am, it astonishes me that men WITH FAMILIES should care to live in this Sodom.

title: Poor Folk
text: For example, there is a family of poor folk who have rented from the landlady a room which does not adjoin the other rooms, but is set apart in a corner by itself.

title: Poor Folk

title: Poor Folk

title: Poor Folk

title: Poor Folk

title: Poor Folk
text: In fact, the thought of these poor people never left me all night, and quite prevented me from sleeping.

title: Poor Folk
text: Well, good-bye, my little Barbara, my little friend beyond price.

title: Poor Folk

title: Poor Folk

title: Poor Folk
text: April 25th

title: Poor Folk
text: MY DEAREST MAKAR ALEXIEVITCH,--Today I met my cousin Sasha. To see her going to wrack and ruin shocked me terribly. Moreover, it has reached me, through a side wind, that she has been making inquiry for me, and dogging my footsteps, under the pretext that she wishes to pardon me, to forget the past, and to renew our acquaintance. Well, among other things she told me that, whereas you are not a kinsman of mine, that she is my nearest relative; that you have no right whatever to enter into family relations with us; and that it is wrong and shameful for me to be living upon your earnings and charity. Also, she said that I must have forgotten all that she did for me, though thereby she saved both myself and my mother from starvation, and gave us food and drink; that for two and a half years we caused her great loss; and, above all things, that she excused us what we owed her. Even my poor mother she did not spare. Would that she, my dead parent, could know how I am being treated! But God knows all about it.... Also, Anna declared that it was solely through my own fault that my fortunes declined after she had bettered them; that she is in no way responsible for what then happened; and that I have but myself to blame for having been either unable or unwilling to defend my honour. Great God! WHO, then, has been at fault? According to Anna, Hospodin [Mr.] Bwikov was only right when he declined to marry a woman who--But need I say it?

title: Poor Folk
text: It is cruel to hear such lies as hers.

title: Poor Folk
text: What is to become of me I do not know.

title: Poor Folk
text: I tremble and sob and weep.

title: Poor Folk
text: Indeed, even to write this letter has cost me two hours.

title: Poor Folk
text: At least it might have been thought that Anna would have confessed HER share in the past.

title: Poor Folk
text: Yet see what she says!

title: Poor Folk
text: For the love of God do not be anxious about me, my friend, my only benefactor.

title: Poor Folk
text: Thedora is over apt to exaggerate matters.

title: Poor Folk
text: I am not REALLY ill. I have merely caught a little cold.

title: Poor Folk

title: Poor Folk
text: Ah, mother, my poor mother!

title: Poor Folk
text: Could you but rise from the grave and learn what is being done to your daughter!

title: Poor Folk
text: May 20th

title: Poor Folk
text: MY DEAREST LITTLE BARBARA,--I am sending you a few grapes, which are good for a convalescent person, and strongly recommended by doctors for the allayment of fever. Also, you were saying the other day that you would like some roses; wherefore, I now send you a bunch. Are you at all able to eat, my darling?--for that is the chief point which ought to be seen to.

title: Poor Folk
text: Let us thank God that the past and all its unhappiness are gone!

title: Poor Folk
text: Yes, let us give thanks to Heaven for that much!

title: Poor Folk
text: As for books, I cannot get hold of any, except for a book which, written in excellent style, is, I believe, to be had here.

title: Poor Folk
text: At all events, people keep praising it very much, and I have begged the loan of it for myself.

title: Poor Folk
text: Should you too like to read it?

title: Poor Folk
text: In this respect, indeed, I feel nervous, for the reason that it is so difficult to divine what your taste in books may be, despite my knowledge of your character.

title: Poor Folk
text: Probably you would like poetry--the poetry of sentiment and of love making?

title: Poor Folk
text: Well, I will send you a book of MY OWN poems.

title: Poor Folk
text: Already I have copied out part of the manuscript.

title: Poor Folk
text: Everything with me is going well; so pray do not be anxious on my account, beloved.

title: Poor Folk
text: What Thedora told you about me was sheer rubbish.

title: Poor Folk
text: Tell her from me that she has not been speaking the truth.

title: Poor Folk
text: Yes, do not fail to give this mischief-maker my message.

text: It is not the case that I have gone and sold a new uniform.

title: Poor Folk

title: Poor Folk

title: Poor Folk
text: Thedora is a vindictive woman--merely a vindictive woman. We shall yet see better days. Only do you get well, my angel--only do you get well, for the love of God, lest you grieve an old man.

title: Poor Folk
text: Also, who told you that I was looking thin?

title: Poor Folk
text: Slanders again--nothing but slanders!

title: Poor Folk
text: I am as healthy as could be, and have grown so fat that I am ashamed to be so sleek of paunch.

title: Poor Folk
text: Would that you were equally healthy!

title: Poor Folk
text: Now goodbye, my angel.

title: Poor Folk
text: I kiss every one of your tiny fingers, and remain ever your constant friend,

title: Poor Folk
text: P.S.--But what is this, dearest one, that you have written to me?

title: Poor Folk
text: Why do you place me upon such a pedestal?

title: Poor Folk

title: Poor Folk
text: How, I repeat?

title: Poor Folk
text: Of course, I might avail myself of the cover of night; but, alas! the season of the year is what it is, and includes no night time to speak of.

title: Poor Folk
text: In fact, although, throughout your illness and delirium, I scarcely left your side for a moment, I cannot think how I contrived to do the many things that I did.

title: Poor Folk

title: Poor Folk
text: Yet, even so, a scandal has arisen.

title: Poor Folk
text: Theresa I trust thoroughly, for she is not a talkative woman; but consider how it will be when the truth comes out in its entirety!

title: Poor Folk

title: Poor Folk
text: Nevertheless, be of good cheer, my beloved, and regain your health.

title: Poor Folk

title: Poor Folk
text: June 1st

title: Poor Folk
text: MY BELOVED MAKAR ALEXIEVITCH,--So eager am I to do something that will please and divert you in return for your care, for your ceaseless efforts on my behalf--in short, for your love for me--that I have decided to beguile a leisure hour for you by delving into my locker, and extracting thence the manuscript which I send you herewith. I began it during the happier period of my life, and have continued it at intervals since. So often have you asked me about my former existence--about my mother, about Pokrovski, about my sojourn with Anna Thedorovna, about my more recent misfortunes; so often have you expressed an earnest desire to read the manuscript in which (God knows why) I have recorded certain incidents of my life, that I feel no doubt but that the sending of it will give you sincere pleasure.

title: Poor Folk
text: Yet somehow I feel depressed when I read it, for I seem now to have grown twice as old as I was when I penned its concluding lines.

title: Poor Folk
text: Ah, Makar Alexievitch, how weary I am--how this insomnia tortures me!

title: Poor Folk
text: Convalescence is indeed a hard thing to bear!

title: Poor Folk
text: UP to the age of fourteen, when my father died, my childhood was the happiest period of my life.

title: Poor Folk
text: It began very far away from here in the depths of the province of Tula, where my father filled the position of steward on the vast estates of the Prince P----.

title: Poor Folk
text: Our house was situated in one of the Prince’s villages, and we lived a quiet, obscure, but happy, life.

title: Poor Folk
text: A gay little child was I--my one idea being ceaselessly to run about the fields and the woods and the garden. No one ever gave me a thought, for my father was always occupied with business affairs, and my mother with her housekeeping. Nor did any one ever give me any lessons--a circumstance for which I was not sorry.

title: Poor Folk
text: At earliest dawn I would hie me to a pond or a copse, or to a hay or a harvest field, where the sun could warm me, and I could roam wherever I liked, and scratch my hands with bushes, and tear my clothes in pieces.

title: Poor Folk
text: For this I used to get blamed afterwards, but I did not care.

title: Poor Folk
text: Had it befallen me never to quit that village--had it befallen me to remain for ever in that spot--I should always have been happy; but fate ordained that I should leave my birthplace even before my girlhood had come to an end.

title: Poor Folk
text: In short, I was only twelve years old when we removed to St. Petersburg.

title: Poor Folk
text: Ah! how it hurts me to recall the mournful gatherings before our departure, and to recall how bitterly I wept when the time came for us to say farewell to all that I had held so dear!

title: Poor Folk
text: I remember throwing myself upon my father’s neck, and beseeching him with tears to stay in the country a little longer; but he bid me be silent, and my mother, adding her tears to mine, explained that business matters compelled us to go.

title: Poor Folk
text: As a matter of fact, old Prince P---- had just died, and his heirs had dismissed my father from his post; whereupon, since he had a little money privately invested in St. Petersburg, he bethought him that his personal presence in the capital was necessary for the due management of his affairs.

title: Poor Folk
text: It was my mother who told me this.

title: Poor Folk
text: Consequently we settled here in St. Petersburg, and did not again move until my father died.

title: Poor Folk
text: How difficult I found it to grow accustomed to my new life!

title: Poor Folk
text: At the time of our removal to St. Petersburg it was autumn--a season when, in the country, the weather is clear and keen and bright, all agricultural labour has come to an end, the great sheaves of corn are safely garnered in the byre, and the birds are flying hither and thither in clamorous flocks. Yes, at that season the country is joyous and fair, but here in St. Petersburg, at the time when we reached the city, we encountered nothing but rain, bitter autumn frosts, dull skies, ugliness, and crowds of strangers who looked hostile, discontented, and disposed to take offence. However, we managed to settle down--though I remember that in our new home there was much noise and confusion as we set the establishment in order.

title: Poor Folk
text: After this my father was seldom at home, and my mother had few spare moments; wherefore, I found myself forgotten.

title: Poor Folk
text: The first morning after our arrival, when I awoke from sleep, how sad I felt!

title: Poor Folk
text: I could see that our windows looked out upon a drab space of wall, and that the street below was littered with filth.

title: Poor Folk
text: Passers-by were few, and as they walked they kept muffling themselves up against the cold.

title: Poor Folk
text: Then there ensued days when dullness and depression reigned supreme.

title: Poor Folk
text: Scarcely a relative or an acquaintance did we possess in St. Petersburg, and even Anna Thedorovna and my father had come to loggerheads with one another, owing to the fact that he owed her money.

title: Poor Folk
text: In fact, our only visitors were business callers, and as a rule these came but to wrangle, to argue, and to raise a disturbance.

title: Poor Folk
text: Such visits would make my father look very discontented, and seem out of temper.

title: Poor Folk
text: For hours and hours he would pace the room with a frown on his face and a brooding silence on his lips.

title: Poor Folk
text: Even my mother did not dare address him at these times, while, for my own part, I used to sit reading quietly and humbly in a corner--not venturing to make a movement of any sort.

title: Poor Folk
text: Three months after our arrival in St. Petersburg I was sent to a boarding-school.

title: Poor Folk
text: Here I found myself thrown among strange people; here everything was grim and uninviting, with teachers continually shouting at me, and my fellow-pupils for ever holding me up to derision, and myself constantly feeling awkward and uncouth.

title: Poor Folk
text: How strict, how exacting was the system!

title: Poor Folk
text: Appointed hours for everything, a common table, ever-insistent teachers!

title: Poor Folk
text: These things simply worried and tortured me.

title: Poor Folk
text: Never from the first could I sleep, but used to weep many a chill, weary night away.

title: Poor Folk
text: In the evenings everyone would have to repeat or to learn her lessons.

title: Poor Folk
text: As I crouched over a dialogue or a vocabulary, without daring even to stir, how my thoughts would turn to the chimney-corner at home, to my father, to my mother, to my old nurse, to the tales which the latter had been used to tell!

title: Poor Folk
text: How sad it all was!

title: Poor Folk
text: The memory of the merest trifle at home would please me, and I would think and think how nice things used to be at home.

title: Poor Folk
text: Once more I would be sitting in our little parlour at tea with my parents--in the familiar little parlour where everything was snug and warm!

title: Poor Folk
text: How ardently, how convulsively I would seem to be embracing my mother!

title: Poor Folk
text: Thus I would ponder, until at length tears of sorrow would softly gush forth and choke my bosom, and drive the lessons out of my head.

title: Poor Folk
text: For I never could master the tasks of the morrow; no matter how much my mistress and fellow-pupils might gird at me, no matter how much I might repeat my lessons over and over to myself, knowledge never came with the morning.

title: Poor Folk
text: Consequently, I used to be ordered the kneeling punishment, and given only one meal in the day.

title: Poor Folk
text: How dull and dispirited I used to feel!

title: Poor Folk
text: From the first my fellow-pupils used to tease and deride and mock me whenever I was saying my lessons.

title: Poor Folk
text: Also, they used to pinch me as we were on our way to dinner or tea, and to make groundless complaints of me to the head mistress.

title: Poor Folk
text: On the other hand, how heavenly it seemed when, on Saturday evening, my old nurse arrived to fetch me!

title: Poor Folk
text: How I would embrace the old woman in transports of joy!

title: Poor Folk
text: After dressing me, and wrapping me up, she would find that she could scarcely keep pace with me on the way home, so full was I of chatter and tales about one thing and another.

title: Poor Folk
text: Then, when I had arrived home merry and lighthearted, how fervently I would embrace my parents, as though I had not seen them for ten years.

title: Poor Folk
text: Such a fussing would there be--such a talking and a telling of tales!

title: Poor Folk
text: To everyone I would run with a greeting, and laugh, and giggle, and scamper about, and skip for very joy.

title: Poor Folk
text: True, my father and I used to have grave conversations about lessons and teachers and the French language and grammar; yet we were all very happy and contented together.

title: Poor Folk
text: Even now it thrills me to think of those moments.

title: Poor Folk
text: For my father’s sake I tried hard to learn my lessons, for I could see that he was spending his last kopeck upon me, and himself subsisting God knows how.

title: Poor Folk
text: Every day he grew more morose and discontented and irritable; every day his character kept changing for the worse.

title: Poor Folk
text: He had suffered an influx of debts, nor were his business affairs prospering.

title: Poor Folk
text: As for my mother, she was afraid even to say a word, or to weep aloud, for fear of still further angering him.

title: Poor Folk
text: Gradually she sickened, grew thinner and thinner, and became taken with a painful cough.

title: Poor Folk
text: Whenever I reached home from school I would find every one low-spirited, and my mother shedding silent tears, and my father raging.

title: Poor Folk
text: Bickering and high words would arise, during which my father was wont to declare that, though he no longer derived the smallest pleasure or relaxation from life, and had spent his last coin upon my education, I had not yet mastered the French language.

title: Poor Folk
text: In short, everything began to go wrong, to turn to unhappiness; and for that circumstance, my father took vengeance upon myself and my mother.

title: Poor Folk
text: How he could treat my poor mother so I cannot understand.

title: Poor Folk
text: It used to rend my heart to see her, so hollow were her cheeks becoming, so sunken her eyes, so hectic her face.

title: Poor Folk
text: But it was chiefly around myself that the disputes raged.

title: Poor Folk
text: Though beginning only with some trifle, they would soon go on to God knows what.

title: Poor Folk
text: Frequently, even I myself did not know to what they related.

title: Poor Folk
text: Anything and everything would enter into them, for my father would say that I was an utter dunce at the French language; that the head mistress of my school was a stupid, common sort of women who cared nothing for morals; that he (my father) had not yet succeeded in obtaining another post; that Lamonde’s “Grammar” was a wretched book--even a worse one than Zapolski’s; that a great deal of money had been squandered upon me; that it was clear that I was wasting my time in repeating dialogues and vocabularies; that I alone was at fault, and that I must answer for everything.

title: Poor Folk
text: Yet this did not arise from any WANT OF LOVE for me on the part of my father, but rather from the fact that he was incapable of putting himself in my own and my mother’s place.

title: Poor Folk
text: It came of a defect of character.

title: Poor Folk
text: All these cares and worries and disappointments tortured my poor father until he became moody and distrustful.

title: Poor Folk
text: Next he began to neglect his health, with the result that, catching a chill, he died, after a short illness, so suddenly and unexpectedly that for a few days we were almost beside ourselves with the shock--my mother, in particular, lying for a while in such a state of torpor that I had fears for her reason. The instant my father was dead creditors seemed to spring up out of the ground, and to assail us en masse. Everything that we possessed had to be surrendered to them, including a little house which my father had bought six months after our arrival in St. Petersburg. How matters were finally settled I do not know, but we found ourselves roofless, shelterless, and without a copper. My mother was grievously ill, and of means of subsistence we had none. Before us there loomed only ruin, sheer ruin. At the time I was fourteen years old. Soon afterwards Anna Thedorovna came to see us, saying that she was a lady of property and our relative; and this my mother confirmed--though, true, she added that Anna was only a very DISTANT relative.

title: Poor Folk
text: Anna had never taken the least notice of us during my father’s lifetime, yet now she entered our presence with tears in her eyes, and an assurance that she meant to better our fortunes.

title: Poor Folk
text: Having condoled with us on our loss and destitute position, she added that my father had been to blame for everything, in that he had lived beyond his means, and taken upon himself more than he was able to perform.

title: Poor Folk
text: Also, she expressed a wish to draw closer to us, and to forget old scores; and when my mother explained that, for her own part, she harboured no resentment against Anna, the latter burst into tears, and, hurrying my mother away to church, then and there ordered Mass to be said for the “dear departed,” as she called my father.

title: Poor Folk
text: In this manner she effected a solemn reconciliation with my mother.

text: Next, after long negotiations and vacillations, coupled with much vivid description of our destitute position, our desolation, and our helplessness, Anna invited us to pay her (as she expressed it) a “return visit.

title: Poor Folk
text: For this my mother duly thanked her, and considered the invitation for a while; after which, seeing that there was nothing else to be done, she informed Anna Thedorovna that she was prepared, gratefully, to accept her offer.

title: Poor Folk
text: Ah, how I remember the morning when we removed to Vassilievski Island!

title: Poor Folk
text: [A quarter of St. Petersburg.] It was a clear, dry, frosty morning in autumn.

title: Poor Folk

title: Poor Folk

title: Poor Folk
text: How terrible it all seemed!

title: Poor Folk
text: AT first--that is to say, until my mother and myself grew used to our new abode--we found living at Anna Thedorovna’s both strange and disagreeable.

title: Poor Folk
text: The house was her own, and contained five rooms, three of which she shared with my orphaned cousin, Sasha (whom she had brought up from babyhood); a fourth was occupied by my mother and myself; and the fifth was rented of Anna by a poor student named Pokrovski.

title: Poor Folk
text: Although Anna lived in good style--in far better style than might have been expected--her means and her avocation were conjectural.

title: Poor Folk
text: Never was she at rest; never was she not busy with some mysterious something or other.

title: Poor Folk
text: Also, she possessed a wide and varied circle of friends.

title: Poor Folk
text: The stream of callers was perpetual--although God only knows who they were, or what their business was.

title: Poor Folk
text: No sooner did my mother hear the door-bell ring than off she would carry me to our own apartment.

title: Poor Folk
text: This greatly displeased Anna, who used again and again to assure my mother that we were too proud for our station in life.

title: Poor Folk
text: In fact, she would sulk for hours about it.

title: Poor Folk
text: At the time I could not understand these reproaches, and it was not until long afterwards that I learned--or rather, I guessed--why eventually my mother declared that she could not go on living with Anna.

title: Poor Folk
text: Yes, Anna was a bad woman.

title: Poor Folk
text: Never did she let us alone.

title: Poor Folk
text: As to the exact motive why she had asked us to come and share her house with her I am still in the dark.

title: Poor Folk
text: At first she was not altogether unkind to us but, later, she revealed to us her real character--as soon, that is to say, as she saw that we were at her mercy, and had nowhere else to go. Yes, in early days she was quite kind to me--even offensively so, but afterwards, I had to suffer as much as my mother.

title: Poor Folk
text: Constantly did Anna reproach us; constantly did she remind us of her benefactions, and introduce us to her friends as poor relatives of hers whom, out of goodness of heart and for the love of Christ, she had received into her bosom.

title: Poor Folk
text: At table, also, she would watch every mouthful that we took; and, if our appetite failed, immediately she would begin as before, and reiterate that we were over-dainty, that we must not assume that riches would mean happiness, and that we had better go and live by ourselves.

title: Poor Folk
text: Moreover, she never ceased to inveigh against my father--saying that he had sought to be better than other people, and thereby had brought himself to a bad end; that he had left his wife and daughter destitute; and that, but for the fact that we had happened to meet with a kind and sympathetic Christian soul, God alone knew where we should have laid our heads, save in the street. What did that woman not say? To hear her was not so much galling as disgusting. From time to time my mother would burst into tears, her health grew worse from day to day, and her body was becoming sheer skin and bone. All the while, too, we had to work--to work from morning till night, for we had contrived to obtain some employment as occasional sempstresses.

title: Poor Folk
text: This, however, did not please Anna, who used to tell us that there was no room in her house for a modiste’s establishment.

title: Poor Folk
text: Yet we had to get clothes to wear, to provide for unforeseen expenses, and to have a little money at our disposal in case we should some day wish to remove elsewhere.

title: Poor Folk
text: Unfortunately, the strain undermined my mother’s health, and she became gradually weaker.

title: Poor Folk
text: Sickness, like a cankerworm, was gnawing at her life, and dragging her towards the tomb.

title: Poor Folk
text: Well could I see what she was enduring, what she was suffering.

title: Poor Folk
text: Yes, it all lay open to my eyes.

title: Poor Folk
text: Day succeeded day, and each day was like the last one.

title: Poor Folk
text: We lived a life as quiet as though we had been in the country.

title: Poor Folk
text: Anna herself grew quieter in proportion as she came to realise the extent of her power over us.

title: Poor Folk
text: In nothing did we dare to thwart her.

title: Poor Folk
text: From her portion of the house our apartment was divided by a corridor, while next to us (as mentioned above) dwelt a certain Pokrovski, who was engaged in teaching Sasha the French and German languages, as well as history and geography--“all the sciences,” as Anna used to say.

title: Poor Folk
text: In return for these services he received free board and lodging.

title: Poor Folk
text: As for Sasha, she was a clever, but rude and uncouth, girl of thirteen.

title: Poor Folk
text: On one occasion Anna remarked to my mother that it might be as well if I also were to take some lessons, seeing that my education had been neglected at school; and, my mother joyfully assenting, I joined Sasha for a year in studying under this Pokrovski.

title: Poor Folk
text: The latter was a poor--a very poor--young man whose health would not permit of his undertaking the regular university course.

title: Poor Folk
text: Indeed, it was only for form’s sake that we called him “The Student.

title: Poor Folk
text: He lived in such a quiet, humble, retiring fashion that never a sound reached us from his room.

title: Poor Folk
text: Also, his exterior was peculiar--he moved and walked awkwardly, and uttered his words in such a strange manner that at first I could never look at him without laughing. Sasha was for ever playing tricks upon him--more especially when he was giving us our lessons.

title: Poor Folk
text: But unfortunately, he was of a temperament as excitable as herself.

title: Poor Folk
text: Indeed, he was so irritable that the least trifle would send him into a frenzy, and set him shouting at us, and complaining of our conduct.

title: Poor Folk
text: Sometimes he would even rush away to his room before school hours were over, and sit there for days over his books, of which he had a store that was both rare and valuable.

title: Poor Folk
text: In addition, he acted as teacher at another establishment, and received payment for his services there; and, whenever he had received his fees for this extra work, he would hasten off and purchase more books.

title: Poor Folk
text: In time I got to know and like him better, for in reality he was a good, worthy fellow--more so than any of the people with whom we otherwise came in contact. My mother in particular had a great respect for him, and, after herself, he was my best friend. But at first I was just an overgrown hoyden, and joined Sasha in playing the fool. For hours we would devise tricks to anger and distract him, for he looked extremely ridiculous when he was angry, and so diverted us the more (ashamed though I am now to admit it). But once, when we had driven him nearly to tears, I heard him say to himself under his breath, “What cruel children!” and instantly I repented--I began to feel sad and ashamed and sorry for him.

title: Poor Folk
text: I reddened to my ears, and begged him, almost with tears, not to mind us, nor to take offence at our stupid jests.

title: Poor Folk
text: Nevertheless, without finishing the lesson, he closed his book, and departed to his own room.

title: Poor Folk
text: All that day I felt torn with remorse.

title: Poor Folk
text: To think that we two children had forced him, the poor, the unhappy one, to remember his hard lot!

title: Poor Folk
text: And at night I could not sleep for grief and regret.

title: Poor Folk
text: Remorse is said to bring relief to the soul, but it is not so.

title: Poor Folk
text: How far my grief was internally connected with my conceit I do not know, but at least I did not wish him to think me a baby, seeing that I had now reached the age of fifteen years.

title: Poor Folk
text: Therefore, from that day onwards I began to torture my imagination with devising a thousand schemes which should compel Pokrovski to alter his opinion of me.

title: Poor Folk
text: At the same time, being yet shy and reserved by nature, I ended by finding that, in my present position, I could make up my mind to nothing but vague dreams (and such dreams I had).

title: Poor Folk
text: However, I ceased to join Sasha in playing the fool, while Pokrovski, for his part, ceased to lose his temper with us so much.

title: Poor Folk
text: Unfortunately this was not enough to satisfy my self-esteem.

title: Poor Folk
text: At this point, I must say a few words about the strangest, the most interesting, the most pitiable human being that I have ever come across.

title: Poor Folk
text: I speak of him now--at this particular point in these memoirs--for the reason that hitherto I had paid him no attention whatever, and began to do so now only because everything connected with Pokrovski had suddenly become of absorbing interest in my eyes.

title: Poor Folk
text: Sometimes there came to the house a ragged, poorly-dressed, grey-headed, awkward, amorphous--in short, a very strange-looking--little old man. At first glance it might have been thought that he was perpetually ashamed of something--that he had on his conscience something which always made him, as it were, bristle up and then shrink into himself.

title: Poor Folk
text: Such curious starts and grimaces did he indulge in that one was forced to conclude that he was scarcely in his right mind.

title: Poor Folk
text: On arriving, he would halt for a while by the window in the hall, as though afraid to enter; until, should any one happen to pass in or out of the door--whether Sasha or myself or one of the servants (to the latter he always resorted the most readily, as being the most nearly akin to his own class)--he would begin to gesticulate and to beckon to that person, and to make various signs.

title: Poor Folk
text: Then, should the person in question nod to him, or call him by name (the recognised token that no other visitor was present, and that he might enter freely), he would open the door gently, give a smile of satisfaction as he rubbed his hands together, and proceed on tiptoe to young Pokrovski’s room.

title: Poor Folk
text: This old fellow was none other than Pokrovski’s father.

title: Poor Folk
text: Later I came to know his story in detail.

title: Poor Folk
text: Formerly a civil servant, he had possessed no additional means, and so had occupied a very low and insignificant position in the service.

title: Poor Folk
text: Then, after his first wife (mother of the younger Pokrovski) had died, the widower bethought him of marrying a second time, and took to himself a tradesman’s daughter, who soon assumed the reins over everything, and brought the home to rack and ruin, so that the old man was worse off than before.

title: Poor Folk
text: But to the younger Pokrovski, fate proved kinder, for a landowner named Bwikov, who had formerly known the lad’s father and been his benefactor, took the boy under his protection, and sent him to school.

title: Poor Folk
text: Another reason why this Bwikov took an interest in young Pokrovski was that he had known the lad’s dead mother, who, while still a serving-maid, had been befriended by Anna Thedorovna, and subsequently married to the elder Pokrovski.

title: Poor Folk
text: At the wedding Bwikov, actuated by his friendship for Anna, conferred upon the young bride a dowry of five thousand roubles; but whither that money had since disappeared I cannot say.

title: Poor Folk
text: It was from Anna’s lips that I heard the story, for the student Pokrovski was never prone to talk about his family affairs.

title: Poor Folk
text: His mother was said to have been very good-looking; wherefore, it is the more mysterious why she should have made so poor a match.

title: Poor Folk
text: She died when young--only four years after her espousal.

title: Poor Folk
text: From school the young Pokrovski advanced to a gymnasium, [Secondary school.] and thence to the University, where Bwikov, who frequently visited the capital, continued to accord the youth his protection.

title: Poor Folk
text: Gradually, however, ill health put an end to the young man’s university course; whereupon Bwikov introduced and personally recommended him to Anna Thedorovna, and he came to lodge with her on condition that he taught Sasha whatever might be required of him.

title: Poor Folk
text: Grief at the harshness of his wife led the elder Pokrovski to plunge into dissipation, and to remain in an almost permanent condition of drunkenness.

title: Poor Folk
text: Constantly his wife beat him, or sent him to sit in the kitchen--with the result that in time, he became so inured to blows and neglect, that he ceased to complain. Still not greatly advanced in years, he had nevertheless endangered his reason through evil courses--his only sign of decent human feeling being his love for his son.

title: Poor Folk
text: The latter was said to resemble his dead mother as one pea may resemble another.

title: Poor Folk
text: What recollections, therefore, of the kind helpmeet of former days may not have moved the breast of the poor broken old man to this boundless affection for the boy?

title: Poor Folk
text: Of naught else could the father ever speak but of his son, and never did he fail to visit him twice a week.

title: Poor Folk
text: To come oftener he did not dare, for the reason that the younger Pokrovski did not like these visits of his father’s.

title: Poor Folk
text: In fact, there can be no doubt that the youth’s greatest fault was his lack of filial respect.

title: Poor Folk
text: Yet the father was certainly rather a difficult person to deal with, for, in the first place, he was extremely inquisitive, while, in the second place, his long-winded conversation and questions--questions of the most vapid and senseless order conceivable--always prevented the son from working.

title: Poor Folk
text: Likewise, the old man occasionally arrived there drunk.

title: Poor Folk
text: Gradually, however, the son was weaning his parent from his vicious ways and everlasting inquisitiveness, and teaching the old man to look upon him, his son, as an oracle, and never to speak without that son’s permission.

title: Poor Folk
text: On the subject of his Petinka, as he called him, the poor old man could never sufficiently rhapsodise and dilate.

title: Poor Folk
text: Yet when he arrived to see his son he almost invariably had on his face a downcast, timid expression that was probably due to uncertainty concerning the way in which he would be received.

title: Poor Folk
text: For a long time he would hesitate to enter, and if I happened to be there he would question me for twenty minutes or so as to whether his Petinka was in good health, as well as to the sort of mood he was in, whether he was engaged on matters of importance, what precisely he was doing (writing or meditating), and so on.

title: Poor Folk
text: Then, when I had sufficiently encouraged and reassured the old man, he would make up his mind to enter, and quietly and cautiously open the door.

title: Poor Folk
text: Next, he would protrude his head through the chink, and if he saw that his son was not angry, but threw him a nod, he would glide noiselessly into the room, take off his scarf, and hang up his hat (the latter perennially in a bad state of repair, full of holes, and with a smashed brim)--the whole being done without a word or a sound of any kind. Next, the old man would seat himself warily on a chair, and, never removing his eyes from his son, follow his every movement, as though seeking to gauge Petinka’s state of mind. On the other hand, if the son was not in good spirits, the father would make a note of the fact, and at once get up, saying that he had “only called for a minute or two,” that, “having been out for a long walk, and happening at the moment to be passing,” he had “looked in for a moment’s rest. Then silently and humbly the old man would resume his hat and scarf; softly he would open the door, and noiselessly depart with a forced smile on his face--the better to bear the disappointment which was seething in his breast, the better to help him not to show it to his son.

title: Poor Folk
text: On the other hand, whenever the son received his father civilly the old man would be struck dumb with joy.

title: Poor Folk
text: Satisfaction would beam in his face, in his every gesture, in his every movement.

title: Poor Folk
text: And if the son deigned to engage in conversation with him, the old man always rose a little from his chair, and answered softly, sympathetically, with something like reverence, while strenuously endeavouring to make use of the most recherche (that is to say, the most ridiculous) expressions.

title: Poor Folk
text: But, alas!

title: Poor Folk
text: He had not the gift of words.

title: Poor Folk
text: Always he grew confused, and turned red in the face; never did he know what to do with his hands or with himself.

title: Poor Folk
text: Likewise, whenever he had returned an answer of any kind, he would go on repeating the same in a whisper, as though he were seeking to justify what he had just said.

title: Poor Folk
text: And if he happened to have returned a good answer, he would begin to preen himself, and to straighten his waistcoat, frockcoat and tie, and to assume an air of conscious dignity.

title: Poor Folk
text: Indeed, on these occasions he would feel so encouraged, he would carry his daring to such a pitch, that, rising softly from his chair, he would approach the bookshelves, take thence a book, and read over to himself some passage or another.

title: Poor Folk
text: All this he would do with an air of feigned indifference and sangfroid, as though he were free ALWAYS to use his son’s books, and his son’s kindness were no rarity at all.

title: Poor Folk
text: Yet on one occasion I saw the poor old fellow actually turn pale on being told by his son not to touch the books.

title: Poor Folk
text: Abashed and confused, he, in his awkward hurry, replaced the volume wrong side uppermost; whereupon, with a supreme effort to recover himself, he turned it round with a smile and a blush, as though he were at a loss how to view his own misdemeanour.

title: Poor Folk
text: Gradually, as already said, the younger Pokrovski weaned his father from his dissipated ways by giving him a small coin whenever, on three successive occasions, he (the father) arrived sober.

title: Poor Folk
text: Sometimes, also, the younger man would buy the older one shoes, or a tie, or a waistcoat; whereafter, the old man would be as proud of his acquisition as a peacock.

title: Poor Folk
text: Not infrequently, also, the old man would step in to visit ourselves, and bring Sasha and myself gingerbread birds or apples, while talking unceasingly of Petinka.

title: Poor Folk
text: Always he would beg of us to pay attention to our lessons, on the plea that Petinka was a good son, an exemplary son, a son who was in twofold measure a man of learning; after which he would wink at us so quizzingly with his left eye, and twist himself about in such amusing fashion, that we were forced to burst out laughing.

title: Poor Folk
text: My mother had a great liking for him, but he detested Anna Thedorovna--although in her presence he would be quieter than water and lowlier than the earth.

title: Poor Folk
text: Soon after this I ceased to take lessons of Pokrovski.

title: Poor Folk
text: Even now he thought me a child, a raw schoolgirl, as much as he did Sasha; and this hurt me extremely, seeing that I had done so much to expiate my former behaviour.

title: Poor Folk
text: Of my efforts in this direction no notice had been taken, and the fact continued to anger me more and more.

title: Poor Folk
text: Scarcely ever did I address a word to my tutor between school hours, for I simply could not bring myself to do it.

title: Poor Folk
text: If I made the attempt I only grew red and confused, and rushed away to weep in a corner.

title: Poor Folk
text: How it would all have ended I do not know, had not a curious incident helped to bring about a rapprochement.

title: Poor Folk
text: One evening, when my mother was sitting in Anna Thedorovna’s room, I crept on tiptoe to Pokrovski’s apartment, in the belief that he was not at home.

title: Poor Folk
text: Some strange impulse moved me to do so.

title: Poor Folk
text: True, we had lived cheek by jowl with one another; yet never once had I caught a glimpse of his abode.

title: Poor Folk
text: Consequently my heart beat loudly--so loudly, indeed, that it seemed almost to be bursting from my breast.

title: Poor Folk
text: On entering the room I glanced around me with tense interest.

title: Poor Folk
text: The apartment was very poorly furnished, and bore few traces of orderliness.

title: Poor Folk
text: On table and chairs there lay heaps of books; everywhere were books and papers.

title: Poor Folk
text: Then a strange thought entered my head, as well as, with the thought, an unpleasant feeling of irritation.

title: Poor Folk
text: It seemed to me that my friendship, my heart’s affection, meant little to him, for HE was well-educated, whereas I was stupid, and had learned nothing, and had read not a single book.

title: Poor Folk
text: So I stood looking wistfully at the long bookshelves where they groaned under their weight of volumes.

title: Poor Folk
text: I felt filled with grief, disappointment, and a sort of frenzy.

title: Poor Folk
text: I felt that I MUST read those books, and decided to do so--to read them one by one, and with all possible speed.

title: Poor Folk
text: Probably the idea was that, by learning whatsoever HE knew, I should render myself more worthy of his friendship.

title: Poor Folk
text: So, I made a rush towards the bookcase nearest me, and, without stopping further to consider matters, seized hold of the first dusty tome upon which my hands chanced to alight, and, reddening and growing pale by turns, and trembling with fear and excitement, clasped the stolen book to my breast with the intention of reading it by candle light while my mother lay asleep at night.

title: Poor Folk
text: But how vexed I felt when, on returning to our own room, and hastily turning the pages, only an old, battered worm-eaten Latin work greeted my eyes!

title: Poor Folk
text: Without loss of time I retraced my steps.

title: Poor Folk
text: Just when I was about to replace the book I heard a noise in the corridor outside, and the sound of footsteps approaching.

title: Poor Folk
text: Fumblingly I hastened to complete what I was about, but the tiresome book had become so tightly wedged into its row that, on being pulled out, it caused its fellows to close up too compactly to leave any place for their comrade.

title: Poor Folk
text: To insert the book was beyond my strength; yet still I kept pushing and pushing at the row.

title: Poor Folk
text: At last the rusty nail which supported the shelf (the thing seemed to have been waiting on purpose for that moment!) broke off short; with the result that the shelf descended with a crash, and the books piled themselves in a heap on the floor!

title: Poor Folk
text: Then the door of the room opened, and Pokrovski entered!

title: Poor Folk
text: I must here remark that he never could bear to have his possessions tampered with.

title: Poor Folk
text: Woe to the person, in particular, who touched his books!

title: Poor Folk
text: Judge, therefore, of my horror when books small and great, books of every possible shape and size and thickness, came tumbling from the shelf, and flew and sprang over the table, and under the chairs, and about the whole room.

title: Poor Folk
text: I would have turned and fled, but it was too late.

title: Poor Folk
text: “All is over!” thought I. “All is over! I am ruined, I am undone! Here have I been playing the fool like a ten-year-old child! What a stupid girl I am! The monstrous fool!”

title: Poor Folk
text: Indeed, Pokrovski was very angry.

title: Poor Folk
text: “What? Have you not done enough?” he cried.

title: Poor Folk
text: “Are you not ashamed to be for ever indulging in such pranks?

title: Poor Folk
text: Are you NEVER going to grow sensible?

title: Poor Folk
text: With that he darted forward to pick up the books, while I bent down to help him.

title: Poor Folk
text: “You need not, you need not!” he went on.

title: Poor Folk
text: “You would have done far better not to have entered without an invitation.”

title: Poor Folk
text: Next, a little mollified by my humble demeanour, he resumed in his usual tutorial tone--the tone which he had adopted in his new-found role of preceptor:

title: Poor Folk
text: “When are you going to grow steadier and more thoughtful? Consider yourself for a moment. You are no longer a child, a little girl, but a maiden of fifteen.”

title: Poor Folk
text: Then, with a desire (probably) to satisfy himself that I was no longer a being of tender years, he threw me a glance--but straightway reddened to his very ears. This I could not understand, but stood gazing at him in astonishment. Presently, he straightened himself a little, approached me with a sort of confused expression, and haltingly said something--probably it was an apology for not having before perceived that I was now a grown-up young person.

title: Poor Folk
text: But the next moment I understood.

title: Poor Folk
text: What I did I hardly know, save that, in my dismay and confusion, I blushed even more hotly than he had done and, covering my face with my hands, rushed from the room.

title: Poor Folk
text: What to do with myself for shame I could not think.

title: Poor Folk
text: The one thought in my head was that he had surprised me in his room.

title: Poor Folk
text: For three whole days I found myself unable to raise my eyes to his, but blushed always to the point of weeping.

title: Poor Folk
text: The strangest and most confused of thoughts kept entering my brain.

title: Poor Folk
text: One of them--the most extravagant--was that I should dearly like to go to Pokrovski, and to explain to him the situation, and to make full confession, and to tell him everything without concealment, and to assure him that I had not acted foolishly as a minx, but honestly and of set purpose.

title: Poor Folk
text: In fact, I DID make up my mind to take this course, but lacked the necessary courage to do it.

title: Poor Folk
text: If I had done so, what a figure I should have cut!

title: Poor Folk
text: Even now I am ashamed to think of it.

title: Poor Folk
text: A few days later, my mother suddenly fell dangerously ill.

title: Poor Folk
text: For two days past she had not left her bed, while during the third night of her illness she became seized with fever and delirium.

title: Poor Folk
text: I also had not closed my eyes during the previous night, but now waited upon my mother, sat by her bed, brought her drink at intervals, and gave her medicine at duly appointed hours.

title: Poor Folk
text: The next night I suffered terribly.

title: Poor Folk
text: Every now and then sleep would cause me to nod, and objects grow dim before my eyes.

title: Poor Folk
text: Also, my head was turning dizzy, and I could have fainted for very weariness.

title: Poor Folk
text: Yet always my mother’s feeble moans recalled me to myself as I started, momentarily awoke, and then again felt drowsiness overcoming me.

title: Poor Folk
text: What torture it was!

title: Poor Folk
text: I do not know, I cannot clearly remember, but I think that, during a moment when wakefulness was thus contending with slumber, a strange dream, a horrible vision, visited my overwrought brain, and I awoke in terror.

title: Poor Folk
text: The room was nearly in darkness, for the candle was flickering, and throwing stray beams of light which suddenly illuminated the room, danced for a moment on the walls, and then disappeared.

title: Poor Folk
text: Somehow I felt afraid--a sort of horror had come upon me--my imagination had been over-excited by the evil dream which I had experienced, and a feeling of oppression was crushing my heart....

title: Poor Folk
text: I leapt from the chair, and involuntarily uttered a cry--a cry wrung from me by the terrible, torturing sensation that was upon me.

title: Poor Folk
text: Presently the door opened, and Pokrovski entered.

title: Poor Folk
text: I remember that I was in his arms when I recovered my senses.

title: Poor Folk
text: Carefully seating me on a bench, he handed me a glass of water, and then asked me a few questions--though how I answered them I do not know.

title: Poor Folk
text: “You yourself are ill,” he said as he took my hand.

title: Poor Folk
text: “You yourself are VERY ill. You are feverish, and I can see that you are knocking yourself out through your neglect of your own health. Take a little rest. Lie down and go to sleep. Yes, lie down, lie down,” he continued without giving me time to protest.

title: Poor Folk
text: Indeed, fatigue had so exhausted my strength that my eyes were closing from very weakness.

title: Poor Folk
text: So I lay down on the bench with the intention of sleeping for half an hour only; but, I slept till morning.

title: Poor Folk
text: Pokrovski then awoke me, saying that it was time for me to go and give my mother her medicine.

title: Poor Folk
text: When the next evening, about eight o’clock, I had rested a little and was preparing to spend the night in a chair beside my mother (fixedly meaning not to go to sleep this time), Pokrovski suddenly knocked at the door.

title: Poor Folk
text: I opened it, and he informed me that, since, possibly, I might find the time wearisome, he had brought me a few books to read.

title: Poor Folk
text: I accepted the books, but do not, even now, know what books they were, nor whether I looked into them, despite the fact that I never closed my eyes the whole night long.

title: Poor Folk
text: The truth was that a strange feeling of excitement was preventing me from sleeping, and I could not rest long in any one spot, but had to keep rising from my chair, and walking about the room.

title: Poor Folk
text: Throughout my whole being there seemed to be diffused a kind of elation--of elation at Pokrovski’s attentions, at the thought that he was anxious and uneasy about me.

title: Poor Folk

title: Poor Folk

What think you, my friend? Shall I go or not? Of course, I should then cease to be a burden to you, and the post appears to be a comfortable one. On the other hand, the idea of entering a strange house appals me. The people in it are landed gentry, and they will begin to ask me questions, and to busy themselves about me. What answers shall I then return? You see, I am now so unused to society--so shy!

title: Poor Folk
text: MY DEAR MAKAR ALEXIEVITCH--No, no, my friend, I must not go on living near you. I have been thinking the matter over, and come to the conclusion that I should be doing very wrong to refuse so good a post. I should at least have an assured crust of bread; I might at least set to work to earn my employers’ favour, and even try to change my character if required to do so. Of course it is a sad and sorry thing to have to live among strangers, and to be forced to seek their patronage, and to conceal and constrain one’s own personality--but God will help me. I must not remain forever a recluse, for similar chances have come my way before.

title: Poor Folk
text: I remember how, when a little girl at school, I used to go home on Sundays and spend the time in frisking and dancing about.

title: Poor Folk
text: Sometimes my mother would chide me for so doing, but I did not care, for my heart was too joyous, and my spirits too buoyant, for that.

title: Poor Folk
text: Yet as the evening of Sunday came on, a sadness as of death would overtake me, for at nine o’clock I had to return to school, where everything was cold and strange and severe--where the governesses, on Mondays, lost their tempers, and nipped my ears, and made me cry. On such occasions I would retire to a corner and weep alone; concealing my tears lest I should be called lazy. Yet it was not because I had to study that I used to weep, and in time I grew more used to things, and, after my schooldays were over, shed tears only when I was parting with friends... It is not right for me to live in dependence upon you. The thought tortures me. I tell you this frankly, for the reason that frankness with you has become a habit. Cannot I see that daily, at earliest dawn, Thedora rises to do washing and scrubbing, and remains working at it until late at night, even though her poor old bones must be aching for want of rest? Cannot I also see that YOU are ruining yourself for me, and hoarding your last kopeck that you may spend it on my behalf? You ought not so to act, my friend, even though you write that you would rather sell your all than let me want for anything. I believe in you, my friend--I entirely believe in your good heart; but, you say that to me now (when, perhaps, you have received some unexpected sum or gratuity) and there is still the future to be thought of.

title: Poor Folk

Though I am bound to you with my whole soul, and love you dearly and strongly and wholeheartedly, a bitter fate has ordained that that love should be all that I have to give--that I should be unable, by creating for you subsistence, to repay you for all your kindness.

title: Poor Folk

title: Poor Folk

Whatsoever you lack here, you have but to ask me for it. Here you love and are loved, and we might easily be happy and contented together. What could you want more? What have you to do with strangers? You cannot possibly know what strangers are like. I know it, though, and could have told you if you had asked me. There is a stranger whom I know, and whose bread I have eaten. He is a cruel man, Barbara--a man so bad that he would be unworthy of your little heart, and would soon tear it to pieces with his railings and reproaches and black looks.

title: Poor Folk
text: On the other hand, you are safe and well here--you are as safe as though you were sheltered in a nest. Besides, you would, as it were, leave me with my head gone. For what should I have to do when you were gone? What could I, an old man, find to do? Are you not necessary to me? Are you not useful to me? Eh? Surely you do not think that you are not useful? You are of great use to me, Barbara, for you exercise a beneficial influence upon my life. Even at this moment, as I think of you, I feel cheered, for always I can write letters to you, and put into them what I am feeling, and receive from you detailed answers.... I have bought you a wardrobe, and also procured you a bonnet; so you see that you have only to give me a commission for it to be executed.... No--in what way are you not useful?

What else would it end in, if you were to go away? Why, in my hiking to the Neva’s bank and doing away with myself. Ah, Barbara, darling, I can see that you want me to be taken away to the Volkovo Cemetery in a broken-down old hearse, with some poor outcast of the streets to accompany my coffin as chief mourner, and the gravediggers to heap my body with clay, and depart and leave me there. How wrong of you, how wrong of you, my beloved! Yes, by heavens, how wrong of you! I am returning you your book, little friend; and, if you were to ask of me my opinion of it, I should say that never before in my life had I read a book so splendid. I keep wondering how I have hitherto contrived to remain such an owl. For what have I ever done? From what wilds did I spring into existence? I KNOW nothing--I know simply NOTHING. My ignorance is complete. Frankly, I am not an educated man, for until now I have read scarcely a single book--only “A Portrait of Man” (a clever enough work in its way), “The Boy Who Could Play Many Tunes Upon Bells”, and “Ivik’s Storks”.

title: Poor Folk
text: MY DEAREST BARBARA ALEXIEVNA--SO much for yesterday! Yes, dearest, we have both been caught playing the fool, for I have become thoroughly bitten with the actress of whom I spoke. Last night I listened to her with all my ears, although, strangely enough, it was practically my first sight of her, seeing that only once before had I been to the theatre. In those days I lived cheek by jowl with a party of five young men--a most noisy crew--and one night I accompanied them, willy-nilly, to the theatre, though I held myself decently aloof from their doings, and only assisted them for company’s sake.

title: Poor Folk

title: Poor Folk

title: Poor Folk
text: MY DEAREST BARBARA ALEXIEVNA,--The book which I received from you on the 6th of this month I now hasten to return, while at the same time hastening also to explain matters to you in this accompanying letter. What a misfortune, my beloved, that you should have brought me to such a pass! Our lots in life are apportioned by the Almighty according to our human deserts. To such a one He assigns a life in a general’s epaulets or as a privy councillor--to such a one, I say, He assigns a life of command; whereas to another one, He allots only a life of unmurmuring toil and suffering.

title: Poor Folk
text: These things are calculated according to a man’s CAPACITY.

title: Poor Folk
text: One man may be capable of one thing, and another of another, and their several capacities are ordered by the Lord God himself.

title: Poor Folk
text: I have now been thirty years in the public service, and have fulfilled my duties irreproachably, remained abstemious, and never been detected in any unbecoming behaviour.

title: Poor Folk
text: As a citizen, I may confess--I confess it freely--I have been guilty of certain shortcomings; yet those shortcomings have been combined with certain virtues.

title: Poor Folk
text: I am respected by my superiors, and even his Excellency has had no fault to find with me; and though I have never been shown any special marks of favour, I know that every one finds me at least satisfactory.

title: Poor Folk
text: Also, my writing is sufficiently legible and clear.

title: Poor Folk
text: Neither too rounded nor too fine, it is a running hand, yet always suitable.

title: Poor Folk

title: Poor Folk

title: Poor Folk

title: Poor Folk

title: Poor Folk

title: Poor Folk
text: No, never!

title: Poor Folk

title: Poor Folk

title: Poor Folk

title: Poor Folk

title: Poor Folk

Is it nothing that, where the pavement is rotten, I have to walk on tiptoe to save my boots? If I write to you overmuch concerning myself, is it concerning ANOTHER man, rather, that I ought to write--concerning HIS wants, concerning HIS lack of tea to drink (and all the world needs tea)?
